Rare ground rupture caught on camera in Kumamoto quake. KUMAMOTO (Jiji Press) -- A security camera in Kumamoto Prefecture has filmed the moment an earthquake in the southwestern Japan prefecture caused the ground to rupture and rise, marking only the second time in the world the phenomenon has been confirmed on video. The footage is "extremely valuable for analyzing the mechanism of earthquakes," Ryusuke Imura, an associate professor of geology at Kagoshima University, said. The video was taken in the city of Yatsushiro, where the 7.1-magnitude July 28 quake recorded a seismic intensity of upper 6, the second-highest level on the Japanese scale, with about 2,500 buildings damaged. It shows a rice paddy and nearby houses rising a few seconds after the shaking began. Imura said that the vertical and horizontal displacement of the fault at the site where the footage was taken totaled roughly 1.2 meters. "We can visually observe the mechanism in which seismic waves arrive first and fault slips appear on the surface a few seconds later," the associate professor said. Imura emphasized that shifts in the ground surface above and around active faults can cause significant damage to buildings, making the footage valuable for disaster prevention. The first confirmed video of the ground rising due to an earthquake was recorded in Myanmar in 2025. While similar videos may have been recorded as security and dashboard cameras have become more widespread, such devices often record over older data after a certain period, making the footage difficult to retrieve. "If there is footage capturing fault offsets, we ask that people save it and share it with us," Imura said. The Kumamoto footage was posted on social media by a 46-year-old man from Yatsushiro after he found it on a security camera at a store run by his younger brother. The post was viewed about 4 million times in a week. "I was surprised that (the post) was viewed more widely than I expected," the man said. "I'm happy if it's useful for research."

Prosecution cites VP Duterte's P2.6-B confidential funds as Davao mayor, but Acosta can't recall it. The House prosecution panel highlighted before the Senate impeachment court on Monday, Aug. 24 the alleged P2.6 billion in confidential funds that respondent Vice President Sara Duterte had at her disposal during her time as Davao City mayor from 2016 to 2022. Private prosecutor Amando Virgil Ligutan confronted hostile witness Gina Acosta with an infographic showing the amounts of confidential funds in Davao City when Duterte--her current boss at the Office of the Vice President (OVP)--was still mayor. The infographic, based on Commission on Audit (COA) records, showed Davao City recorded over P2.6 billion in confidential expenses from 2016 through 2022, covering Duterte’s six years as mayor: P144 million in 2016, P294 million in 2017, P420 million in 2018, and P460 million annually from 2019 through 2022. Acosta handled the then-mayor’s confidential funds and later transferred them to the OVP, where she also handled the same funds as special disbursement officer (SDO). However, when asked if she knew about the P460 million in secret funds Davao City had annually in those four years, Acosta said she could not remember such allocations. She attributed her age for her difficulty in remembering such details to her age, which she said were from years ago. “Contributor po ang edad ko, Your Honor, at saka dugay na po na, matagal na, Your Honor,” she said. (My age contributed to it, Your Honor, and it has been a long time already, Your Honor.) “You don't remember that. All in all, from 2019 to 2022, simple math will tell us: P1,840,000,000, almost P2 billion confidential funds sa Davao City binigay, hindi n'yo rin maalala yung total na 'yan. Tama po ba?” Ligutan said. (You don’t remember that. All in all, from 2019 to 2022, simple math will tell us: P1,840,000,000, almost P2 billion in confidential funds were given to Davao City, and you also don’t recall that total. Is that correct?) The amount of secret funds Vice President Duterte had as Davao City mayor dwarfed the P612.5 million in confidential funds in 2022 and 2023 to the OVP and to the Department of Education (DepEd) when she was education secretary. The OVP received a total of P500 million, while P112.5 million was released to DepEd. Acosta testified that she released the entire P500 million in four tranches to then OVP security officer Col. Raymund Dante Lachica upon Duterte’s orders. Lachica was then commander of the Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group (VPSPG). He was later let go from his post following the controversy over the alleged misuse of OVP and DepEd confidential funds. His DepEd counterpart, Col. Dennis Nolasco, allegedly received the department’s secret funds from the agency’s SDO, Edward Fajarda. Fajarda has been subpoenaed to testify in the Vice President’s trial. However, the impeachment court presiding officer Senator Francis “Chiz” Escudero, announced on Monday that Fajarda sent a letter from a law firm informing the court that he suffered a stroke and wished to excuse himself from the trial.

500 TODA members join Las Piñas cleanup. Five hundred members of various tricycle operators and drivers’ associations (TODA) in Las Piñas City have been deployed to their respective barangays to carry out community cleanup activities under the Tulong Panghanapbuhay sa Ating Disadvantaged/Displaced Workers (TUPAD) program. Mayor April Aguilar said the beneficiaries have started their 10-day work assignment, where they will assist in cleaning creeks, public markets, roads, and other areas identified by the city government. Aguilar said that some of the workers were deployed with personnel from the City Environment and Natural Resources Office (CENRO) to help clear and clean creeks as part of the city’s efforts to maintain clean waterways and reduce the risk of flooding. She said that others were assigned to cleanup activities in public markets and along roads in their respective barangays. The mayor said that each beneficiary will receive P755 per day for 10 days, or a total of P7,550, for the services they render under the program. She said that Public Employment Service Office (PESO) head Red Garcia and Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) Muntinlupa-Parañaque-Las Piñas (Muntaparlas) Director Jeremiah Carlos, conducted the orientation before the workers were deployed. The city government said the program provides temporary employment assistance while mobilizing workers to help maintain the cleanliness of communities. Aguilar reminded the beneficiaries to perform their assigned duties responsibly and work closely with barangay and city personnel throughout their 10-day engagement.

Shirley Kuan on why she left Bea Alonzo: 'I was given no choice'. Bea Alonzo’s former manager, Shirley Kuan, has opened up about why she decided to quit as Bea Alonzo's manager. At a press conference, Shirley clarified that the final straw was when she was "disinvited" to an event for the actress, something that "offended" her mainly because she claimed she "closed the deal" herself. “I closed this event deal; I was talking to the client and preparing this event. I was told by the client that I’m disinvited, and I already knew what happened even when the client didn’t want to tell me. I already knew who it is,” Shirley said. The veteran talent manager maintained she has no idea what led to it but accepted the decision. “Hindi ako nagalit, but I’ll be a hypocrite if I tell you I’m not offended because this was never done to me. Wala naman akong kasalanan, what have I done?” "That’s the last straw. After I told her that, she said she didn’t know about it. ‘Okay, now I’m telling you. And this very moment and as of this very day, I’m no longer your manager,” she said. Shirley also shared how she communicated with Bea prior about the constant bashing she was getting for supposedly meddling with her wedding plans to Vincent Co. “Ang sabi ko hindi ko alam kung bakit ako sinisiraan non-stop, Bea, you never defended me. Hindi mo naman ako ipinagtanggol,” Shirley said. Shirley then clarified why she decided to speak about the issue. “I promised her I’m not going to make any announcement about any resignation. But I was given no choice but to defend myself because enough is enough. I kept quiet, I kept my promise, until it came out. Was it yesterday? I was in the news everywhere." Bea is yet to issue a statement on the matter.

Japan’s Foreign Minister emphasizes important role of ICC. TOKYO, Aug. 24 (Jiji Press) -- Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi emphasized the importance of the International Criminal Court, in a video message to a meeting of Asian and African officials in Tokyo on Monday. Motegi did not mention the sanctions imposed last week by the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump against ICC President Tomoko Akane of Japan. The ministry did not disclose when the message was recorded. "Japan attaches great importance to the role of international judicial institutions in the peaceful settlement of disputes and the maintenance of legal order, and has been actively engaged in strengthening these institutions," Motegi said in the video. "Our collective efforts are reflected in the presidency of both the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court being held by Japanese judges," he also said. "As the international order that we have built is under an array of challenges, we are living in a critically important era that will determine whether the international community as a whole can defend a free and open international order based on the rule of law," the minister noted. The meeting marked the opening of the Tokyo International Law Seminar, an international law training event hosted by the ministry. The seminar will run until Friday, featuring lectures by researchers.

Michelin expands Philippine distribution network after over 60% volume growth. Michelin Philippines is accelerating its local expansion after growing its business by more than 60 percent in volume since 2023, as the French tire manufacturer bets on the country’s long-term market potential. The company appointed three new specialized importer-distributors—Bermaz Auto Philippines, Icon Equipment Solutions Philippines Inc., and BSB Junrose Corp.—bringing its importer network in the country to seven. They join Drakester Inc., Entire Car Care Centre Inc., RYCO Inc., and Tiara Commercial & Industrial Corp. Michelin Philippines and Pacific Islands managing director Jonathan Khong told a press conference on Monday, Aug. 24, that the company remains optimistic about the Philippine market, citing opportunities in industries such as mining, agriculture, transportation, and logistics. Khong said Michelin considers the country’s challenging road conditions when determining which products to offer in the local market. “In a country where there are more challenging road conditions, for example, we will sell a different tire. So to answer your question, we [do] take into consideration, in fact, the road conditions whenever we make a tire available for sale in that country,” he told Manila Bulletin in a separate interview. Rather than treating difficult road conditions as a barrier to sales growth, Michelin uses its engineering and tire technology to offer products suited to local operating conditions. The company is also seeing rapid changes in how Filipino consumers purchase tires, particularly through e-commerce. Khong said the Philippines is at the forefront of this shift, with Filipino consumers buying tires online at one of the fastest rates compared with other markets in the region. Meanwhile, rising raw material and freight costs as well as foreign exchange (forex) fluctuations continue to exert pressure on the tire business. Khong said Michelin seeks to keep its products competitive by emphasizing the value they provide, even if the company does not necessarily offer the cheapest tires in the market. - Danielle T. Bayani

170,000 tons of treated water released from Fukushima plant. TOKYO, Aug. 24 (Jiji Press) -- About 170,000 tons of treated water has been released from Tokyo Electric Power Company Holdings Inc.'s meltdown-hit Fukushima No. 1 nuclear plant in northeastern Japan, TEPCO said Monday, three years after the releases began. According to TEPCO, some 39 trillion becquerels of radioactive tritium contained in the treated water have been discharged into the ocean during the period from the plant devastated by the March 2011 powerful earthquake and tsunami. As of this month, about 1.23 million tons of water are stored at the plant, including treated water kept in on-site tanks, down by over 7 pct from the level before the discharges began. In the 2011 accident, scorching hot nuclear fuel that could not be cooled had melted down inside the No. 1, No. 2 and No. 3 reactors of the plant, with some dripping to the bottom of containment vessels. Water is still being injected into the reactors. Tainted water, or water injected into the reactors that has come into contact with the melted nuclear fuel, accumulates in the basement of the reactor buildings. The amount of such water also increases due to rainwater and groundwater flowing into the buildings. For this reason, the amount of tainted water stored at the plant does not drop by as much as the amount of water discharged from the facility into the ocean. The concentration of radioactive materials in the tainted water is significantly reduced by an advanced liquid processing system, or ALPS. As tritium cannot be removed from the water easily, the treated water has been diluted by mixing seawater before being released into the ocean. Tritium, a radioactive substance that emits weak beta rays, has a half-life of about 12 years and is found in nature. TEPCO has set its annual tritium release limit at 22 trillion becquerels. The company said that tritium levels in nearby waters are regularly measured and remain below the operational threshold.

Northern boobook flies non-stop from Japan to the Philippines - research. TOKYO, Aug. 25 (Jiji Press) -- Tracking with a GPS device has revealed that a northern boobook, an owl species, flew more than 1,800 kilometers nonstop over the sea from Japan to the Philippines, according to a study by a research team including Japan's Tohoku University. The owl species is about 30 centimeters in body length. In Japan, it lives in a wide range of places, except areas including the Ogasawara Islands, remote Tokyo islands in the Pacific, and breeds in locations such as parks in urban areas in summer. Although it has been found that the owl species spends winter in Southeast Asia, its migratory routes have not been known in detail. For the study, the researchers attached small GPS data loggers to four northern boobooks that lived in Sendai, the capital of Miyagi Prefecture, northeastern Japan. An analysis last summer of data collected from one of the four showed that the male bird traveled south over the Japanese archipelago in late October 2024. It then flew 1,848 kilometers from Cape Sata, Kagoshima Prefecture, southwestern Japan, to the Philippine island of Luzon nonstop over the sea in a 36-hour trip in early November the same year. The owl later spent some four months on the Indonesian island of Kalimantan during winter before traveling some 1,500 km to the southern China island of Hainan in late March 2025. After flying north over continental China, it returned to Sendai in late April. The study "revealed a new aspect of owls running counter to people's notion that they don't move," said Yawara Takeda, a Tohoku University researcher specializing in developmental biology. "If its migratory routes and resting locations are identified, that would help preserve the species," Takeda said. The study was published in a British scientific journal in June.

Kraken’s swan song: What prompts Fajardo to think about Gilas retirement. Gilas Pilipinas is heading to a battle that is not only important for its implications to the country’s World Cup but also extra special as it could also be the swan song for one of its pillars. June Mar Fajardo has hinted about a possible retirement from Gilas duty at the end of the crucial August window of the 2027 FIBA World Cup qualifiers. The 6-foot-10 center actually even had a lengthy speech to the rest of the team at the end of the last window before Cone convinced him to play for one more window in the second round of the qualifiers. It was a decision that came as a surprise not only from the fans but even for head coach Tim Cone and the rest of his teammates. “Posible. Posibleng last two games ko na ito with Gilas,” said Fajardo. But for Fajardo, the decision didn’t take much thinking, especially with his body already feeling the aches and bruises of the 14 years of juggling his duties between Gilas and San Miguel in the PBA. “Matanda na ako,” added the 36-year-old gentle giant. More than the age, however, Fajardo said he just wants to take care of his body and give himself enough time to rest and recover – something he will not be able to do with Gilas games usually happening in the offseason. The SMB center even had a major injury in the past when he sustained a broken tibia largely due to the physical toll of playing for both Gilas and the Beermen in the PBA. “Nung time kasi na iyon pinagpapahinga na ako ng doctor kasi nga nakita na na may hairline (fracture) yung tibia ko. Hindi naman pwede iyon kasi sa San Miguel umabot rin kami sa finals,” said Fajardo, recalling the injury that sidelined him for almost two years. “Na-take ko ‘yun as positive na baka iyon na ‘yung nagsasabi na yung katawan ko na kailangan ko magpahinga. Ngayon, ayoko isagad yung katawan ko. Gusto ko pa maglaro ng basketball. Nag eenjoy pa ako maglaro ng basketball. And di ko na maeenjoy iyon kung may masakit na iniinda,” he explained. Fajardo said he is already content with his Gilas experience, even considering himself blessed to win a gold in the Asian Games and be part of the 2023 World Cup after recovering from the nasty injury. “Sobrang blessed ko nga na nakabalik pa ako kasi after nga na mabali yung tibia ko, naisip ko nga na di na ako makakabalik non sa basketball. Yun yung lowest of lowest ko,” said Fajardo who was also part of the two previous World Cup squads in 2014 and 2019. “Nabigyan ulit ako ng second chance. Sobrang blessed ako na nakasali uli ako sa national team. Nakasali pa ako sa Asian Games na nag-gold, nag World Cup pa ako after nung incident,” he added.

Calamity victims need not prove they’re poor to get aid, says DSWD. The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) on Tuesday, Aug. 25, reminded families affected by calamities that they do not have to prove that they are poor before they can receive humanitarian assistance from the agency. DSWD-Disaster Response and Management Group Assistant Secretary Irene Dumlao said families affected by disasters are not required to secure a certificate of indigency to access emergency assistance. She explained that local government units (LGUs), as frontline responders, are responsible for identifying and assessing the number of people and families affected by a disaster. “Kung matatandaan natin, ang local government units ang frontline in service delivery, sila nga po yung nangunguna na nagbibigay ng tulong sa kanila pong mga nasasakupan na naapektuhan ng mga iba’t ibang mga kalamidad (As we remember, local government units are the frontline in service delivery. They are the ones who lead in providing assistance to their constituents affected by various calamities),” Dumlao said. The data gathered by LGUs helps determine which families need assistance and what type of support should be provided, she added. The DSWD then augments the assistance provided by LGUs and extends technical support in responding to calamities and other emergencies. The clarification comes as the government continues to assist communities affected by the enhanced southwest monsoon or “habagat” and tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay, and Neneng. As of Tuesday, DSWD said it had provided at least ₱1.2 billion worth of humanitarian assistance to affected communities. The assistance included about 1.9 million family food packs, ready-to-eat food boxes, non-food items, and ₱14.4 million in financial assistance for families severely affected by the recent weather disturbances.

Why vaccines are good for your heart. As an infectious diseases doctor, I take every opportunity to tout the life-saving efficacy of vaccines. Many of my medical colleagues feel the same way. Pulmonologists are among the most enthusiastic vaccinators of adults, especially against respiratory diseases like pneumonia, influenza, and respiratory syncytial viruses (RSV). Subspecialities that deal with immunocompromised patients are another big group of vaccinators. This includes endocrinologists who see a lot of diabetic patients, nephrologists who see a lot of dialysis patients, and oncologists who take care of people with cancer, especially those undergoing chemotherapy. Geriatricians are also conscientious vaccinators since elderly patients are a major at-risk group for vaccine-preventable diseases. Primary care providers such as internists and family practitioners do routine immunizations, especially for flu and pneumonia. Obstetricians immunize pregnant women to protect both mother and baby against vaccine-preventable diseases such as tetanus and RSV. Many cardiologists act as primary care providers and so they are likely to vaccinate as well. In addition, there are an increasing number of cardiac diseases that can benefit from vaccination. With more people developing coronary artery disease and heart failure, vaccination has made its way into cardiology clinical practice guidelines. Recognizing this trend, both the American College of Cardiology and the European Society for Cardiology recently came up with clinical consensus statements advocating the use of vaccination in preventing major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Cardiologists are among the earliest adopters of evidence-based medicine. Each anti-hypertensive, each anti-coagulant, and each cardioprotective medication needs to have a wealth of evidence behind it before it can be adopted into their guidelines. The fact that both American and European cardiology groups decided to come out with specific statements supporting vaccination means that there is compelling evidence for vaccines in protecting patients with cardiac diseases. Which vaccines do the cardiologists recommend? The American and European consensus statements are similar, although the American statement endorses more vaccines. Both strongly recommend the use of influenza vaccination and Covid-19 vaccination for the prevention of MACE in those with heart disease. In addition, the American statement also explicitly recommends pneumococcal vaccination with newer formulations (PCV 20 or PCV 21) for 19 years old and above among those with chronic heart disease while the European statement still considers the use of older pneumococcal vaccine formulations (PCV13 and PPSV23) with variable minimum ages of administration. RSV vaccination at 60 years old and older (recently modified to 50 years old and older), and shingles vaccination at 50 years old and older for those with cardiac disease are recommended by the American consensus statement while the European guidelines are equivocal about the minimum age of recommendation for RSV and shingles administration pending the results of additional ongoing clinical trials. Influenza vaccination Influenza vaccination is recommended for everyone more than six months old in the US and in the Philippines regardless of risk factors. In Europe, different countries have different recommendations but almost all of them recommend that elderly persons get an annual influenza vaccination. Influenza infection is associated with a six-fold increased risk of myocardial infarction (heart attack) in the general population. Both consensus statements recommend annual flu vaccination for people with existing cardiac diseases because they are at higher risk for influenza and the complications of influenza. There is strong evidence that getting the flu shot in this population further decreases the risk of heart attacks, stroke, decompensated heart failure and hospitalization. Pneumococcal vaccination Pneumococcal vaccination prevents the development of pneumonia and its complications caused by specific strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae, the most common bacterial cause of pneumonia. Pneumococcal pneumonia can be deadly especially for the elderly and can be complicated with endocarditis (infection of the heart valves) and meningitis (infection of the membranes surrounding the brain). There are two kinds of pneumococcal vaccines: polysaccharide and conjugated vaccines. The polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) has historically contained more strains than the conjugate vaccine (PCV) but is considered a less effective vaccine. The conjugate vaccine elicits a stronger immune response. PPSV23 requires a booster after five years while the most recent vaccines (PCV20 and PCV21) only require a single dose for life. A combination of the old PCV13 vaccine plus PPSV23 is considered a lifetime vaccination according to the European guidelines, although they can still receive an additional dose of PCV20 or PCV21. The American guidelines explicitly recommend a single dose of PCV20 of PCV21 for those who have not received a vaccine previously. The age for pneumococcal vaccination for the general population is 50 years old and older in the US and in the Philippines. Among those with chronic medical conditions, the vaccine can be administered from age 19 onwards. These medical conditions include a number of cardiac diseases including congestive heart failure, chronic heart disease and cardiomyopathies (diseases of heart muscle). Covid-19 vaccination Covid-19 vaccination was recommended for everyone during the pandemic, and it continues to be recommended for those who have not been vaccinated. It is especially important for people with heart problems because they are three times more likely to get severe Covid-19. Updated vaccines have not been available in the Philippines, but they continue to be recommended in the US for elderly and at-risk populations. One heart-related controversy that came out was the rare side effect of mRNA vaccines causing myocarditis in young males. However, this side effect was usually mild, and getting Covid-19 infection is associated with a six-fold higher risk of myocarditis than the vaccine. Other non-mRNA vaccines did not seem to cause myocarditis and can be used for young males as an alternative. There is evidence that preventing Covid-19 with vaccines decreases the overall risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, atrial fibrillation (a type of arrhythmia), and yes, even myocarditis and pericarditis overall. RSV While RSV is a lesser-known virus than influenza, it can be deadlier than influenza and Covid-19 among unvaccinated populations. The elderly and those with congestive heart failure and other cardiac ailments are particularly vulnerable to this seasonal virus. There are currently three approved vaccines for RSV, two of which are available in the Philippines. A recent randomized-controlled trial found that RSV vaccination reduced all-cause cardiorespiratory hospitalizations in adults 60 years or older. RSV vaccination is currently recommended in those 50 years old and above in the US. Herpes Zoster (Shingles) Shingles is a reactivation of previous chickenpox infection that causes a significant inflammatory state that is known to increase the risk of stroke and cardiac events. Zoster vaccination has been shown to decrease the risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, congestive heart failure and arrhythmia for at least eight years (possibly more) after vaccination. Those with preexisting coronary artery disease seem to benefit even more than the general population. The current recommendation is for adults in the general population 50 years old and older to receive two doses of the vaccine. The shingles vaccine is available in the Philippines and is more than 90 percent effective at preventing shingles and the protection lasts at least 11 years. Doctors and scientists are seeing more and more links between the development of cardiac disease and infections. The inflammation that occurs in response to an infection can push someone with preexisting heart problems into a heart attack or stroke. Therefore, it makes sense that preventing infections with vaccines will be good for the heart.

‘Filipiñana’ proves Filipino cinema isn’t dead. After clips from Rafael Manuel's debut film went viral on X, many were quick to claim the Philippines just found its own Wes Anderson. While the synchronized style and unique framing do give off similar vibes, Rafael’s latest film is so much more than a Wes Anderson tribute of sorts. It’s a testament to how Filipino cinema is likely the next big thing foreign viewers start yearning for. Already, “Filipiñana” has gained recognition in the US after nabbing the Special Jury Award for Creative Vision at the Sundance Film Festival and landing Rafael the New Directors Award at the San Francisco International Film Festival. Europeans were also able to share their views on the film after its run at the recent Berlinale. Now, “Filipiñana” faces its homecourt, with select cinemas screening it nationwide starting today. Perfect timing, given the recent discourse surrounding Filipino films and their quality. Starting with its strengths, almost every shot is aesthetically pleasing to look at. Not a single frame feels dull due to the careful thought put into shooting each scene. A truly remarkable job done by cinematographer Xenia Patricia. There’s also a satisfying feeling from watching the synchronized movements of the actors in some settings, like when a row of golfers line up their shots or in the opening montage where we are shown the club’s daily operations. During an advanced screening talkback session, it was revealed how the crew shot in eight different golf courses to craft the setting. Yet, it all feels as if it’s set in one place. It also evokes a certain nostalgic effect due to the yesteryear vibe of the brutalist architecture featured throughout. In the film, we follow two leads, Isabel (Jorrybell Agoto) and Clara (Carmen Castellanos). Isabel shows us the perspective of the working class whose gruntwork keeps the golf course running, while Clara gives us the perspective of the upper class, being one of the club members’ nieces visiting the country for a round of golf before heading off to college in the US. These two largely different paths show us the interesting socioeconomics that play out within Filipino golf course and country club settings. “So many people have to keep (golf courses) maintained and beautiful, but ultimately, only a few people get to enjoy it,” shares Rafael upon reflecting on his film. “It’s a really good representation of our country.” Some minor background characters also give us humorous or curious moments that seem minuscule at first, but lead to quite the pay-off later on. Beautiful as it is to see the spectacle that plays throughout, viewers will likely have strong opinions about the film’s slow pace. Some might feel scenes overstay their welcome. This slowness, however, does feel somewhat meditative. Catching glimpses of the two characters’ lives makes us wonder a lot about their stories, and we become invested in their little journey within the golf course. A lot of mystique also revolves around the seemingly elusive golf course owner, Dr. Palanca (Teroy Guzman). “Filipiñana,” however, is not the type of film that holds your hand and gives an easy-to-digest pay-off by the end. Chances are you’ll find yourself appreciating the immersive experience or looking at the clock now and then as you wait for things to get a move on. There is no in-between. A lot of buzz has also come around regarding the film’s potential to be a future submission to the Oscars. While highly possible, the production team remains humble about this endeavor, simply proud of the already successful run it had at the Sundance Film Festival and the Berlinale. After all, a submission to The Academy takes up a lot of resources since it requires passing it around to voting members and ensuring it gets good distribution worldwide. Fortunately, from the team’s response, they’re highly thankful for the international distributors they have helping spread the word in Europe and the US. What's wonderful about a film like “Filipiñana” being made is that it gives local independent cinema a fighting chance. A slow-burner film being made here shows that we are willing to take risks on producing quality films that focus more on artistic integrity rather than just box office numbers. If local filmmakers like Rafael continue to receive support from local producers, distributors, and the government, we can continue to create films that may very well surpass international arthouse icons like Wes Anderson, Jean-Luc Godard, Andrei Tarkovsky, and so on. We already know, based on reactions from international audiences from film festivals held abroad, that there is a global yearning to see more Filipino movies. It’s high time to push forward our support for local cinema so that it can continue to thrive and bring in more curious viewers from all over. “Filipiñana” is now showing at SM Cinemas in SM Megamall, SM North EDSA, SM Mall of Asia, SM Aura, SM Fairview, and SM Seaside.

Philta exec confirms Eala’s Asiad participation. It’s confirmed. World No. 18 Alex Eala will be playing in the 2026 Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya, making September a brutal month for one of Asia’s athletic wonders. No less than Philippine Tennis Association Secretary-General and Navotas Mayor John Rey Tiangco confirmed Eala’s participation in the continental showpiece, where she is fancied to deliver a precious medal for the country. “Yes,” was the short but definitive reply from the former junior tennis standout to a question that boggled many minds after it was disclosed that the WTA Asian swing – three big tournaments – would be held in conflict with the quadrennial event. The tennis competition at the 20th Asian Games begins on Sept. 27 at the Nagoya City Higashiyama Park Tennis Center, which is the last day of the Singapore Open – it will start on Sept. 21. Other Asian tournaments scheduled during the Asian Games are the Korea Open (Sept. 21-27) and the China Open (Sept. 30-Oct. 11). There were reports that Eala was most likely to vie in Singapore, with posters of Eala and American Jessica Pegula already all over the rich island nation. Though Eala is expected to maintain her lofty ranking, she can’t afford to skip the Asian Games since the champion of the event can secure a continental qualification berth for the Los Angeles Olympics. In the coming Asian Games, Eala will be aiming to improve on her two-bronze medal show – one each in singles and mixed doubles – at the Covid-delayed Hangzhou Games in China three years ago. Eala, 21, won those medals as a rising star. Now that she’s regarded as one of the global stars, the charming Filipina is likely to author another first in her glowing record books.

Romualdez tells Ombudsman: Apply evidence rule or dismiss complaints. Former House Speaker, Leyte 1st district Rep. Martin Romualdez is pressing the Office of the Ombudsman to make up its mind whether or not the supposed evidence it has against him can stand on its legs. In the 25-page Supplemental Counter-Affidavit Ex Abundanti Ad Cautelam, filed last Thursday, Aug. 20, Romualdez argued that the Ombudsman cannot file a case first and then leave serious conflicts in sworn accounts for a trial court to sort out later. In particular, the Lakas-Christian Muslim Democrats (Lakas-CMD) president asked the Ombudsman to weigh a case that now includes 32 sworn statements. These include three recantations, two supporting statements, 25 new affidavits of denial and non-participation, the earlier sworn statement of Allan Colesio – an ex-aide of former Ako Bicol Party-list Rep. Zaldy Co – and Senate Blue Ribbon Committee Orly Guteza’s recantation. Romualdez said that together, the statements challenge the personal knowledge and credibility of witnesses used to connect him to alleged deliveries of cash-filled suitcases that were supposedly payoffs for anomalous or "ghost" flood control projects. As such, the Ex-Speaker asked the Ombudsman to identify what admissible, credible, and preservable evidence remains after the recantations and direct denials. If that record cannot meet the agency’s own rule, Romualdez said, the complaints should be dismissed. The Ombudsman earlier said that it was looking at possible plunder charges against Romualdez. The ad cautelam ("for caution") filing argues that the Ombudsman must weigh those challenges under its own 2026 Revised Rules of Procedure before filing any Information. On page 16 of the filing, Romualdez stated, “Faced with these statements that cast doubt on the truth of the allegations in the Complaints, this Honorable Office cannot have basis to satisfy the standard of prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction required under Section 3, Rule V of the 2026 Ombudsman Rules of Procedure.” The filing argues that this threshold is higher than the former probable-cause standard. On page 22, it stated, “The evidentiary standard of prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction was deliberately designed to elevate, and not merely restate, the former standard of probable cause.” The Ombudsman’s official rule requires prosecutors to evaluate the full record, including a respondent’s counter-affidavit. Contrasting the new rule with the old standard, the filing stated on page 22 that “The former expressly requires this Honorable Office to already assess admissibility and credibility before an Information may issue, not to defer that assessment to trial.” The supplemental filing also reproduced the rule’s definition. It stated that the “entirety of evidence presented by the parties is (a) admissible, (b) credible, and (c) capable of being preserved and presented to establish all the elements of the crime or offense, as well as the identity of the person or persons responsible therefor.” The supplemental filing stressed that language makes credibility an immediate duty. On page 22, Romualdez stated, “Admissibility and credibility are thus not concerns reserved for the trial court; they are integral to this Honorable Office’s own determination of whether a case should be filed at all.” The filing says the changed record includes alleged delivery companions who deny taking part, former aides who deny knowledge of cash deliveries, three witnesses who withdrew earlier statements, and Guteza who disowned the alleged eyewitness link to Romualdez. It also says no contractor has stated that money was paid to Romualdez, no DPWH official has said he demanded or received a kickback, no identified project has been traced to a payment to him, and no financial record has traced alleged unlawful proceeds to his assets. The ad cautelam filing further stated, “This is not a matter that can be set aside for resolution at some future trial; it is a defect in the evidence as it stands today, and it is precisely the kind of defect that Section 3, Rule V was written to catch before an Information is ever filed.”

Marcos to health institutions: Ensure that no Filipino is denied healthcare due to financial woes. Emphasizing that financial constraints can prevent families from accessing appropriate and better treatment, President Marcos called on healthcare institutions to ensure that no Filipino is denied treatment due to financial limitations. "We encourage more hospitals across the country to support PhilHealth in advancing Universal Health Care by embracing the No Co-Payment Policy. Together, let us ensure that no Filipino is denied the care that they need only because of financial hardship," Marcos said in his speech on Tuesday, Aug. 25. The President witnessed the signing of a memorandum of agreement (MOA) between PhilHealth and St. Luke’s Medical Center–Global City for the implementation of benefit packages and policies for PhilHealth members. Under the agreement, St. Luke's allocated 53 beds, allowing PhilHealth members to seek specialized treatment at the hospital under the no-balance billing program. With the agreement, Marcos said patients "will no longer be scared" to seek treatment at private hospitals. "Kaya kahit na yung dati na hindi nakakapunta sa private hospital kagaya ng St. Luke's ay matutulungan na makapunta rito at bibigyan natin ng suporta galing—yung kagaya ng dati sa PhilHealth, sa DOH, at sa kung minsan kahit sa Office of the President (So, those who previously cannot go to private hospitals like St. Luke's, will be able to seek treatment at will be given support from PhilHealth, Department of Health, and from the Office of the President)," Marcos said in an interview after the signing ceremony. "Pero ito ay para hindi na matatakot ang mga nagkakasakit na pumunta sa private hospital dahil wala silang pambayad (This is so that patients will no longer be scared to go to private hospital because they cannot afford it)," Marcos added. According to Marcos, the partnership between the governent and private hospitals will be further expanded. "Paparamihin pa natin ‘yan para lahat na talaga ng ating mga facilities, healthcare facilities ay kasama na sa mga programa natin para kahit na hindi lang yung mga may kaya ang makakapunta sa ating mga private hospital para makakuha sila nung specialized na healthcare na kung minsan ay kinakailangan nila ngunit wala silang pambayad kaya hindi sila lumalapit at hindi sila nagpapatingin sa ating mga private hospital (We will expand this further so that all of our healthcare facilities will be included in our programs, ensuring that specialized healthcare is accessible not only to those who can afford it, but also to those who need it but cannot afford to pay. Sometimes, people do not seek consultation or treatment at private hospitals because they cannot afford the cost)," Marcos said. The President said the MOA between PhilHealth and St. Luke’s Medical Center-Global City "sends an important message that quality care in leading private hospitals can be made more accessible to qualified PhilHealth members, and that both government and the private sector have a role in making Universal Health Care work." "Malinaw ang ating hangarin. Hindi dapat maging hadlang ang kakulangan sa pera para makakuha ang kinakailangang atensiyong medical (Our objective is clear. Financial limitations should not hinder someone to get the needed medical attention)," Marcos said. "It is a simple yet universal belief that we must all uphold," he added. The Chief Executive further called on healthcatre institutions to continue to ensure that the country's healthcare system "becomes more responsive and affordable for Filipino families, especially those who are most in need." He called on them to continue removing the financial, geographic, and institutional barriers that keep patients from getting the assistance that they need.

Pasig facility highlights PH-Japan elderly care ties. The Pasig Magokoro Elderly Care Facility highlighted the continuing Philippines-Japan cooperation in strengthening elderly care and improving services for senior citizens. Japanese government and Department of Health (DOH) officials visited the facility on Aug. 20 as part of the 4th Philippines-Japan High-Level Joint Committee Meeting (HLJCM), which included elderly care, universal health coverage, and disaster health management among its major areas of cooperation. Ambassador for Global Health Teiji Hayashi led the Japanese delegation, which included representatives from the Cabinet Secretariat, Embassy of Japan, and Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), while the DOH was represented by officials from the Bureau of International Health Cooperation, National Center for Geriatric Health, and DOH-Metro Manila Center for Health Development. Pasig City officials welcomed the delegation, led by the city mayor, who expressed the local government's appreciation to Japan and JICA for their cooperation in establishing the Magokoro Elderly Care Facility. The mayor also cited the contributions of the partner agencies in sharing their knowledge and experience in elderly care, noting that the facility is only the beginning of the city's broader goal of providing better and more humane services for senior citizens. City Social Welfare and Development Office Head Ma. Teresa Briones presented the facility's programs and services, including its Japanese-style caregiving concept. The site visit was part of Philippines‑Japan health cooperation, focusing on senior citizen services and sharing healthcare knowledge and practices. The Philippines-Japan health cooperation began with a Memorandum of Cooperation signed by the DOH and its Japanese counterparts on Feb. 21, 2019, aimed at strengthening collaboration between the two countries in various areas of healthcare.

Sustain high public trust, satisfaction ratings, Nartatez tells PNP commanders. Gen. Jose Melencio C. Nartatez, Jr., chief of the Philippine National Police (PNP), ordered all police commanders to regularly review the efficiency of their peace and order strategic implementation in order to sustain the high public trust and satisfaction ratings of the police. Nartatez issued the order after the release of the OCTA Research survey for the second quarter of 2026, 65 percent of adult Filipinos trust the PNP, higher than the 63 percent recorded in March 2026. The same survey also indicated that 63 percent of respondents were satisfied with the PNP’s performance, up from 61 percent in the first quarter of the year. Nartatez commended police personnel, saying the rise in public trust and satisfaction ratings would have not been possible had it not been for their dedication, professionalism and commitment to serve and protect the Filipino people. “The trust and satisfaction ratings obtained by the Philippine National Police (PNP) in a recent survey should serve as a motivation to do more in order for the public to feel the hard work and sacrifices of every police officer in keeping all streets and communities safe,” said Nartatez. “To serve and protect the Filipino people is the mandate of your PNP and doing them with honor, compassion and integrity is a commitment that we continue to pursue and strengthen,” he added. Nartatez said the figures also affirm the efficiency of the police force as an organization and proof that the wisdom behind the Enhanced Managing Police Operations (EMPO) has been effective and working well. He noted that the improved ratings should not lead police personnel to become complacent, instead, inspire them to further improve police services and strengthen the PNP’s response to the public. Following the result of the survey, Nartatez said he expects all police commanders down to the station levels to study the survey result and review the existing crime prevention measures to identify the gaps and further improve the peace and order measures. “Maintaining peace and order is a continuing process that needs constant review and adjustments,” said Nartatez. “The goal has always been to make the Filipino people feel every decline in crime rate—and we are thankful that this is being appreciated with high trust and satisfaction ratings,” he added.

Ice Seguerra to fans uploading full concert performances online: 'Please don't turn our work into content'. Ice Seguerra appealed to fans to stop uploading full concert performances online, reminding concertgoers that purchasing a ticket does not give them the right to reproduce or distribute footage of the entire show. The singer-songwriter made the appeal in a Facebook post on Monday, Aug. 24, following the recent staging of "Sessionistas: The Playlist" at The Theatre at Solaire on Aug. 22. The concert featured Ice alongside Sitti Navarro, Nyoy Volante, Kean Cipriano, Princess Velasco and Juris, with Ice also serving as the show's director. While he appreciate fans who record and share memorable moments from concerts, he drew the line at uploading entire performances or lengthy portions of a show. “When you buy a concert ticket, you're buying the experience of watching the show. You are not buying the right to record the whole thing and upload it to your own YouTube page or social media pages,” Ice wrote. The singer also emphasized the point in Filipino: “Hindi po dahil nakabili tayo ng ticket, atin na rin ang concert.” Ice noted that a concert involves the work of numerous people, including artists, musicians, composers, producers, publishers, and crew members. “That work is protected, and reposting full songs or entire portions of a concert without permission is not simply ‘sharing.’ It is an unauthorized distribution of someone else's work,” Ice said. Instead, Ice encouraged fans to share photos, short video clips, and their personal reactions to the shows. “Please share your favorite moments. Post your photos. Post short clips. Tell people what you loved about the show. We appreciate all of that. But please don't upload the concert itself,” he said. Ice also appealed to fans who have already posted full performances from their shows to take the videos down. “To those who have uploaded full performances from our shows, I'm asking you to please take them down,” Ice said. “Support the music. Support the artists,” Ice added. “Please don't turn our work into content you never had the right to distribute.” Ice's wife and "Sessionistas: The Playlist" creative director Liza Diño has also addressed the issue, warning that legal action could be pursued against unauthorized uploads. “We will be protecting the rights of our artists and our productions, and we will take the necessary steps against unauthorized uploads when needed,” Diño said. She likewise encouraged concertgoers to support artists without reproducing their work without permission, ending her comments with “Support artists by sharing the experience. Please don't steal the work.”

ABAP wary of Asiad medal chances; PH boxers to train in Bangkok and Nagoya. Association of Boxing Alliances in the Philippines (ABAP) President Marcus Manalo remains wary of the boxing team’s chances in the 2026 Asian Games in Japan next month despite fielding an elite squad spearheaded by Olympic medalists. "Looks good on paper but all Olympic medalists had very limited tournament participation since the (2024 Paris) Olympics,” Manalo told Manila Bulletin/Tempo. The Asiad-bound team is spearheaded by two-time Olympic medalist Nesthy Petecio, 2020 Tokyo Games silver medalist Carlo Paalam and 2024 Paris Olympics bronze medalist Aira Villegas. Also joining the squad are Norlan Petecio, Junmilardo Ogayre and Riza Pasuit. Despite the concern, Manalo remains confident that the team can deliver, particularly with the regith preparation in the final stretch leading up to the Asiad. The team is scheduled to hold training camps in Bangkok, Thailand and Nagoya, Japan, where boxers will spend two weeks training in Bangkok before moving to Nagoya for a week ahead of the competition, which is set for Sept. 21 to Oct. 2 at the Nishio City General Gymnasium in Aichi, Japan. “They just really have to focus on this last month of preparation in Bangkok and Nagoya,” Manalo said. Boxing has been the country’s source of gold mine in the Asian Games, with Filipino fighters collecting 15 gold, 10 silver and 31 bronze medals since the sport was introduced in 1954. The country’s last Asiad gold, however, came in the 2010 Guangzhou Games through Rey Saludar. In the previous edition in Hangzhou, China, the Philippines settled for one silver medal, courtesy of Eumir Marcial. Marcial, however, will skip this year’s Games due to a scheduling conflict with his professional fight.

Sandiganbayan denies Uswag Ilonggo congressman’s motion to consolidate graft case. ILOILO CITY—The Sandiganbayan has denied the plea of USWAG Ilonggo party-list Rep. James “Jojo” Ang Jr. to consolidate the14 counts of graft cases for alleged conflict of interests in government infrastructure projects. “Ang's motion for consolidation is hereby denied for lack of merit,” wrote the Sandiganbayan Sixth Division in a resolution dated August 24, 2026. Last July 25, the Office of the Ombudsman filed 14 separate counts of graft against Ang for having financial interest in Allencon Development Corp., which won P214 million worth of contracts with the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) in Iloilo and Antique. Records from the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) found that Ang was still a stockholder of Allencon until March 29, 2023, a period wherein he was already a party-list congressman after winning a seat during the May 2022 elections. “Although the said cases appear to be similar in nature, it is undeniable that each case involves a project separate and distinct from the others,” the Sandiganbayan said in its August 24 decision. “It is improbable that there will be conflicting rulings on factual matters. Furthermore, instead of expediting the proceedings, consolidation will merely cause delay,” the Sandiganbayan added. Ang was also alleged to be previously tied to International Builders Corp. (IBC), the biggest contractor in Western Visayas. Both Allencon and IBC are reportedly owned by the family of Alfonso Tan, the uncle of Ang. Since Ang was linked to the flood control scandal last year, he has remained largely quiet. There were instances that he did issue a public statement. “I am one with the people in exacting accountability from those responsible for robbing our people of their hard-earned taxes and eroding the integrity of our institutions,” Ang said in a September 2025 public statement.

Denmark's prime minister blasts unsolicited beauty advice from plastic surgeon on Instagram. COPENHAGEN, Denmark (AP) — Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen is fed up with getting unsolicited beauty advice. The 48-year-old wrote Monday on Instagram that she had just returned back home from a trip to Ukraine, where she was exposed to air raid sirens in the ongoing war, only to find a message by a plastic surgeon offering her to “fix that little spot on your nose.” “I’ve lost count of how many messages I’ve received over the years about my appearance,” Frederiksen wrote. “Especially that I have ugly teeth and thin hair. That I have an ugly ‘wart’ on my nose and well-meaning advice to get some Botox.” The prime minister of the Nordic country posted a screen shot of the plastic surgeon's offer on Instagram but without identifying him. She also posted her response: “Oh no. I’m happy with my body — I really don’t need a male plastic surgeon to have an opinion about it!” Frederiksen, a Social Democrat and Denmark ’s second female prime minister, is now in her third term, making her one of Europe's longest-serving and most experienced leaders. She has led the European Union and NATO member country since mid-2019. She has pledged to maintain a firm stance against U.S. President Donald Trump’s ambitions for Greenland, the kingdom’s semiautonomous territory, and continue supporting Ukraine against Russia's war of aggression. On Instagram, Frederiksen stressed that she does not interfere with other people's looks and that “I’m perfectly fine with my body — as it is when you’re a woman approaching 50.” She added that "if you’re going to write to me (and you’re more than welcome to), I hope you’ll use your time to talk about something more meaningful. Not my nose." The prime minister also said that those unsolicited beauty tips and suggestions made her feel “indignant” and that “today, I’m sending an extra loving thought to all of you who have to put up with the 'perfect imperfections' we all walk around with every day.”

Indonesia intensifies aerial firefighting as wildfire haze spreads to Malaysia. JAKARTA, Indonesia (AP) — Indonesia intensified its ground and aerial firefighting operations Monday as huge blazes in central and western regions scorched wide areas of forests and peatland, creating a choking haze that blanketed cities and crossed borders. Indonesian police have arrested 72 people suspected of starting some of the forest and peatland fires, while four companies are under investigation for allegedly using fire to clear land at low cost. Emergency services have been battling fires driven by an intensifying El Nino pattern and a prolonged dry season, generating dense smoke that crossed into Malaysia and Brunei, according to the National Disaster Management Agency, or BNPB. Fires remained active in several regions on Monday, according to the agency, while large-scale suppression efforts continue in fire-prone provinces including West, Central and South Kalimantan on Borneo island and in Riau, South Sumatra and Jambi on Sumatra island. The fires are part of a broader surge in wildfire activity across Indonesia this year. Drought, strong winds and dry vegetation have complicated efforts to contain the fires, the BNPB said in a statement. Some hot spots remained inaccessible to more than 24,000 ground firefighters who were deployed on Sumatra and Borneo, prompting local officials to request additional water-bombing support. Prabowo visits fire-affected areas After visiting areas devastated by forest and peatland fires in Central Kalimantan on Saturday, President Prabowo Subianto traveled to fire-affected Riau and its neighboring province of South Sumatra on Monday, where more than 36,000 hectares (89,000 acres) have burned in 10 provinces, to encourage authorities to get the haze cloud under control. Prabowo vowed the government would continue supporting firefighting operations, including through the deployment of additional water-bombing helicopters and oxygen supplies for firefighters. He urged the authorities to “thoroughly document and report the work being carried out by firefighting teams” directly to him. Prabowo also called for stronger public education and outreach efforts, saying the central government will deploy about 1,000 military and police officers to work alongside regional authorities in raising awareness and preventing forest and land fires. The latest satellite data from the Environment Ministry showed South Sumatra recorded the highest number of hot spots nationwide with 1,429, followed by West Kalimantan with 1,226 and Central Kalimantan with 811. East Kalimantan logged 576 hot spots, ahead of Riau with 503, while West Papua and Jambi recorded 468 and 458 hot spots, respectively. Forestry Ministry data indicated that nearly 94,000 hectares (232,000 acres) were burned in July alone. The Transportation Ministry said it has authorized the use of 35 foreign-registered aircraft to support wildfire response operations, including water-bombing missions and aerial patrols. The ministry said the aircraft can be rapidly redeployed to disaster-hit areas as conditions change, while complying with Indonesian aviation safety regulations. Indonesia and Malaysia boost cloud seeding against wildfires Indonesia is actively intensifying weather-modification operations to help firefighters combat wildfire by inducing rainfall through the dispersal of salt particles into suitable clouds, with 30 aircraft for water-bombing and cloud-seeding over Kalimantan and another 22 helicopters covering Sumatra. Malaysia said on Monday that Indonesia has granted permission for its aircraft to enter Indonesian airspace to conduct cloud-seeding operations along their shared border as the two neighbors step up efforts to tackle the worsening haze. Malaysia is preparing an operational plan and could also offer help to Indonesia to fight fires if requested, Environment Minister Arthur Joseph Kurup said, adding that the measures were critical to ensure air quality improves as Malaysia prepares to celebrate National Day on Aug. 31 to mark independence from British rule. Commemorations for the annual Malaysia Day on Sept. 16 — marking the nation's unification — will be held in the eastern state of Sarawak on Borneo, one of the areas most affected by the haze, Kurup said. Nearly 600 schools in Sarawak were closed last week as air quality deteriorated, affecting about 200,000 students, while officials expect hot and dry conditions to persist into October. Fires are a regular problem during the dry season in Indonesia, a vast archipelago nation of more than 17,000 islands, with often strained relations with neighbors. Plantation owners and traditional farmers often start fires to clear land for farming, triggering hazardous haze that reduces visibility, disrupts land and air transportation and threatens public health, sometimes affecting neighboring countries in Southeast Asia.

Tricycle driver dies after fallen tree pins him down inside his vehicle in Ilocos Sur. STA. MARIA, Ilocos Sur — A tricycle driver died after an acacia tree fell on him while he was sleeping inside his vehicle at the Innanus TODA Parking Area on Dakota Street in Barangay Poblacion Sur here on Monday, Aug. 24. Police Lt. Jenson Refuerzo, officer-in-charge of the Sta. Maria Municipal Police Station, identified the victim as alias “Rod”, 45, a resident of the area. Refuerzo said the incident occurred at about 3 p.m. when police received a report of a fallen tree at the parking area, where two tricycles were hit. Responding officers immediately arrived at the scene and found the victim trapped under the tree and his vehicle. Several tricycle drivers told police that they noticed the tree beginning to fall and immediately warned people in the area to evacuate. However, the victim apparently failed to hear the warning because he was asleep inside his tricycle. Refuerzo said the entire acacia tree fell directly onto the tricycle, killing the driver instantly. Authorities believe that continuous rainfall may have softened the soil, causing the acacia tree to topple.

A political amnesty law takes effect in Thailand but excludes lese majeste. BANGKOK (AP) — An amnesty for political offenses committed in Thailand over the past two decades took effect Monday, but the law excludes some of the more serious cases, including those involving lese majeste, or defaming the monarchy. The amnesty was introduced to promote reconciliation after past political instability, violent protests and military coups and could cover about 6,000 people, according to estimates made in Parliament. But the exclusion of lese majeste offenses has drawn criticism that the amnesty will not truly resolve political divisions. The Peaceful Society Promotion Act passed a final vote by lawmakers in July and was published in the Royal Gazette on Sunday. A committee chaired by the prime minister will determine who qualifies for the amnesty. The committee must hold its first meeting within 30 days, although it's unclear how long the process will take. The law covers a range of offenses related to political activities from Jan. 1, 2005 to July 15, 2025. It will not only grant release for current prisoners, but also close investigations and prosecutions, dismiss pending court cases, and clear criminal records of those eligible for the amnesty. In addition to lese majeste, the amnesty will also exclude corruption and crimes resulting in death or serious injury. The lese majeste law, also known as Article 112 of the Criminal Code, is controversial not only because it has been used to punish things as simple as liking a post on Facebook, but also because anyone — not just royals or the authorities — can lodge a complaint that most of the time leads to detention during lengthy legal proceedings. A conviction of defaming the monarchy carries a prison term of up to 15 years, and critics say Article 112 has often been used to quash political dissent. Student-led pro-democracy demonstrations starting in 2020 sought reforms of the lese majeste law, but the protesters became targets of the law. Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, a law advocacy group, says more than 290 people, many of them student activists, have been charged with violating Article 112 since early 2020. As of July, the group said at least 54 people remained imprisoned in connection with political cases. Only about 10 were expected to benefit from the new amnesty, since the others were accused of lese majeste. Thailand’s machinery of state remains deeply conservative. Its political establishment is sensitive about any perceived threats to the status of the monarchy. The country’s political conflicts revolved mostly around former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, who was ousted by a military coup in 2006. His populist policies won strong support among poorer voters, particularly in the rural north and northeast, but his popularity and sometimes high-handed style created deep fractures between his base and the country’s urban elites, royalists and the military. Violent protests and political upheaval repeatedly followed as parties aligned with Thaksin returned to power while he remained in self-imposed exile.

FDCP to mark 50 years of PH cinema’s second golden age. The Film Development Council of the Philippines (FDCP) will mark the 50th anniversary of the second golden age of Philippine Cinema with a month-long program of film screenings, festivals and industry events in September. The Philippine Film Industry Month (PFIM) 2026, themed “Pelikula: Ginintuang Ikalawa,” will look back at the filmmakers and films associated with the period from the mid-1970s to the late 1980s while also highlighting new filmmakers and current developments in the local industry. The month opens on Sept. 4 with a screening of the 4K digitally restored “Tinimbang Ka Ngunit Kulang” (1974), directed by National Artist Lino Brocka, at Red Carpet Cinema in Shangri-La Plaza. The opening event will also include the announcement of the Philippines’ entry to the 99th Academy Awards, or the Oscars, through the Film Academy of the Philippines. Among the classic films scheduled for screening at FDCP Cinematheque Centres nationwide are Mike De Leon’s “Itim” (1976), Brocka’s “Insiang” (1976), Mario O’Hara’s “Tatlong Taong Walang Diyos” (1976), Lupita Aquino-Kashiwahara’s “Minsa’y Isang Gamu-Gamo” (1976), Eddie Romero’s “Ganito Kami Noon... Paano Kayo Ngayon?” (1976) and Ishmael Bernal’s “Nunal sa Tubig” (1976). The Philippine Film Archive will also present “SineUna: Cinematic Action Before the War,” featuring surviving Filipino films made before World War II, including “Zamboanga” (1937), “Giliw Ko” (1939), “Tunay na Ina” (1939), “Pakiusap” (1940) and “Ibong Adarna” (1941). At Cinematheque Centre Manila, “Reel to Real: Pelikula at Panayam” will feature Brocka’s “Jaguar” (1979) on Sept. 9, while the September edition of the Director’s Series will focus on Jeffrey Jeturian and screen “Tuhog” (2001) and “Kubrador” (2006) on Sept. 10. Canada to announce retaliatory tariffs as Trump tells its leaders to ‘fall in line’. TORONTO (AP) — Canada will announce retaliatory tariffs against the United States on Tuesday after relations deteriorated sharply Monday, with President Donald Trump telling Canadian leaders to “fall in line” or face consequences “far WORSE” than existing tariffs and Prime Minister Mark Carney accusing Washington of trying to subordinate Canada. Trump also threatened new 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel, while Carney said U.S. trade demands showed Washington wanted to “destroy our major industries,” including autos, steel and aluminum. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne and three other Cabinet ministers are also expected Tuesday morning to share details of supports for workers affected by tariffs. Carney said earlier Monday that Canada may need to move away from matching U.S. tariffs dollar for dollar and instead use more targeted retaliation aimed at protecting Canadian workers and businesses. “An attitude at the negotiation table that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States” is “not something we’re going to accept,” Carney said. Carney was even more blunt in French. “We learned during the negotiations that the Americans want to destroy our major industries, including autos, steel and aluminum,” Carney said. “That was one of the main reasons we said no. It was a bad deal.” The fiery words from both sides show how U.S.-Canada relations have deteriorated since Carney walked away from trade negotiations with the Trump administration late Friday, triggering the president’s threatened 50% tariffs the next day on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods. Canada and the United States share one of the world’s largest trading relationships, with deeply integrated supply chains across autos, energy, agriculture and manufacturing, making a prolonged trade fight potentially costly for businesses and workers on both sides of the border. Carney cast doubt on the U.S.’s dependability, saying Canada was finding reliable partners “everywhere in the world, except in the United States. Except in the United States. And Russia.” Trump unleashes personal attacks on Canadian leaders On Monday, Trump came back with further tariffs, warning that he would impose them on Canada's auto industry beginning next year. “Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years,” Trump wrote on social media, criticizing what he called the country’s “ridiculously high tariffs” on American farmers. Carney said Washington’s auto-sector proposals would gradually have the effect of dismantling Canadian production. “This is the most successful automotive partnership in history,” Carney said, referring to the deeply integrated Canada-U.S. industry. Meanwhile, Ontario Premier Doug Ford unleashed his own tirade. In an interview with The Associated Press, he said Trump had underestimated Canadians’ willingness to endure economic pain rather than give in to U.S. pressure. “We’re all in,” Ford said. “Up here, we’re at a fever pitch; everyone’s in for an economic war. They know they’re going to have to sacrifice.” Trump responded in a social media post by attacking Ford personally, calling him “the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford,” and once again referring to Canada's prime minister as “Governor Carney.” Ford dismissed the insults: “If you think an insult from him hurts me? Well, bring it on, buddy, I’m ready.” Ford is a Progressive Conservative whose party differs from that of Carney, a Liberal, but the two underscore broad political unity in Canada over the trade fight with Trump. Ford threatens critical minerals and electricity Ford said “everything is on the table” if the dispute worsens, including cutting off electricity and critical minerals from Ontario. Critical minerals are increasingly important to U.S. national security and manufacturing. The Pentagon has sought more secure supplies of minerals used in military aircraft, missiles, munitions and electronics as Washington tries to reduce reliance on China, which dominates the mining or processing of several strategically important minerals. Ford said Canada should also consider increasingly severe retaliation if Trump continues targeting Canadian industries, including oil and potash, while Ontario could raise electricity prices or stop sending power south. “We power 1.5 million homes and businesses,” Ford said. “Everything’s on the table. I’ll do whatever it takes.” Ford has used electricity as leverage before. During an earlier phase of the dispute, Ontario imposed a 25% surcharge on electricity exported to Michigan, Minnesota and New York. Trump responded by threatening to double tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum before both sides backed away. Auto industry becomes a central battleground Ford accused Trump of not simply seeking a better trade deal but aiming to hollow out Canadian industries and move production south. Ford said Trump wants to make Canada a vassal state. “He wants to bleed out every single sector and bring them down to the U.S.,” Ford said. The auto sector is especially important to Ontario, the center of Canada’s vehicle manufacturing industry. Plants and suppliers in Ontario are tightly integrated with factories in Michigan and other U.S. states, with parts routinely crossing the border multiple times during production. Automakers including Ford, General Motors and Stellantis operate major assembly plants in Ontario, and the wider supply chain supports tens of thousands of jobs. Trump’s new threat of a 50% tariff on Canadian vehicles and parts puts that sector directly at the center of the escalating dispute. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Monday that “the only reason Canada has auto production in the first place” was because of the 1960s Auto Pact, under which Canada used access to its market to encourage vehicle production north of the border. Ford says he opposed preliminary deal Ford also disclosed that he had opposed the preliminary agreement Carney was considering before Canada walked away from negotiations, and that he was unwilling to restore American liquor to Ontario store shelves as part of an agreement. “I wasn’t going to put the booze back on the shelves,” Ford said. “I was ready to go out there and call a press conference … and say I’m not buckling over.” Ford said he understood Washington had sought language late in the negotiations that would have restricted Canada’s ability to negotiate trade agreements with other countries without U.S. approval. Carney has called that demand unacceptable and a question of Canadian sovereignty. Carney said the dispute also exposed a deeper divide over language and culture, saying protections for French and Canadian culture that Washington views as trade irritants are considered fundamental rights in Canada. “Who does he think he is?” Ford said of Trump. “You gotta be kidding.”
